{{Short description|American physicist (1922–2007)}}
'''James "Jim" Ricker Wilson''' (October 21, 1922, [[Berkeley, California]] – August 14, 2007, [[Livermore, California]]) was an American theoretical physicist, known for his pioneering research in numerical relativity and 
numerical relativistic hydrodynamics.<ref name=ObitPT>{{cite magazine|author=May, Michael|author2=Van Bibber, Karl|author3=Mathews, Grant|doi=10.1063/PT.4.2161|title=Obituary of James Ricker Wilson |magazine=Physics Today |volume=61|issue=3|page=70|date=September 14, 2007 }}</ref>

==Biography==
After graduating in 1942 with a B.S. degree in chemistry from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] (UC Berkeley),<ref name=BethePrize>{{cite web|title=2007 Hans A. Bethe Prize Recipient, James R. Wilson|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Wilson&first_nm=james&year=2007}}</ref> he served in the U.S. Army, working in a minor role on the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory#The Manhattan Project|Manhattan Project at Los Alamos]].<ref name=CarefulConvert>{{cite magazine|author=Smith, Marika Wilson|title=The Careful Convert|magazine=Notre Dame Magazine|date=Autumn 2009|url=https://magazine.nd.edu/stories/the-careful-convert/}}</ref> After working at Los Alamos from 1944 to 1946 he returned as a graduate student in physics to UC Berkeley. There he received his Ph.D. in 1952.<ref name=BethePrize/> His Ph.D. thesis entitled ''Some problems in meson theory'' was supervised by Roland Hamilton Good (1923–2010),<ref>{{cite web | url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=150269 | title=James Ricker Wilson |website=Physics Tree}}</ref> who was elected in 1958 a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (APS).<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1958&unit_id=&institution=Iowa+State+College}} (search on year=1958 and institution=Iowa State College)</ref> After working for a year from 1952 to 1953 at Albuquerque's [[Sandia National Laboratories|U.S. Army Sandia Laboratory]], Wilson became in 1953 a staff member of the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]], where he worked until shortly before his death at age 84.<ref name=BethePrize/><ref name=CarefulConvert/> From 1968 to 1969 he spent a sabbatical year at the [[University of Cambridge]], where he began his study of astrophysics. From 1996 to 2007 he was also an adjunct professor of physics at the [[University of Notre Dame]],<ref name=ObitPT/> which he often visited.<ref name=CarefulConvert/>

In the first two decades of his career he applied his expertise in computational physics to classified projects involving nuclear weapons. In the 1970s and 1980s [[Hans Bethe]] often visited Livermore and collaborated with Wilson on core-collapse supernovae.<ref name=ObitPT/>

In 1994 he received the Marcel Grossmann Prize. He was a member of the APS and the [[American Astronomical Society]]. In 2007 he received the [[Hans A. Bethe Prize]] with citation:

Wilson was an enthusiastic rock climber and mountaineer. In 1947 he met his future wife Demetria "Dee' Corombos (1922–2005) on a rock climbing expedition in Wyoming's [[Wind River Range]],<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/eastbaytimes/name/demetra-wilson-obituary?id=26305091 | title=Demetra Corombos Wilson, Obituary (2005) East Bay Times | website=[[Legacy.com]] }}</ref> and their love of mountains was "one of their strongest bonds."<ref name=CarefulConvert/> They were married in February 1949<ref name=ObitPT/> in a Greek Orthodox Church in [[Oakland, California]]. They were members of the Bay Area chapter of the [[Sierra Club]]'s rock-climbing section and regularly went on local climbs.<ref name=CarefulConvert/> The couple had five children and annually took a weeklong family backpacking trip in the [[Sierra Nevada]].<ref name=ObitPT/>

Upon his death in 2007 he was survived by five children, seventeen grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/eastbaytimes/name/james-wilson-obituary?id=24647233 | title=James Ricker Wilson, Obituary (2007) East Bay Times | website=[[Legacy.com]] }}</ref>

James Ricker Wilson should not be confused with James Randall Wilson, who was elected in 2001 a fellow of the APS.<ref name=APS>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2001&unit_id=&institution=Princeton+Plasma+Physics+Laboratory}} (search on year=2001 and institution=Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory)</ref>
